c063.front: When can you not change data through a view?
c063.back: When the view has group functions (for example SUM), GROUP BY, DISTINCT, ROWNUM or set operators (UNION…). Then one view row does not correspond to one table row. INSERT also fails when the view leaves out a NOT NULL column without a DEFAULT value.
c063.try_sql:
-- A view with GROUP BY and MAX: one view row is many table rows
UPDATE (SELECT department_id, MAX(salary) AS max_sal
        FROM   employees
        GROUP  BY department_id)
SET    department_id = 50;

c064.front: How does WITH CHECK OPTION differ from WITH READ ONLY?
c064.back: WITH CHECK OPTION: you can change data through the view, but a new or changed row must still satisfy the view's WHERE. WITH READ ONLY: you can change nothing through the view; no INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE gets through.
c064.try_sql:
-- After the change the row would fall out of the view's WHERE, so CHECK OPTION rejects it
UPDATE (SELECT employee_id, department_id
        FROM   employees
        WHERE  department_id = 30
        WITH CHECK OPTION)
SET    department_id = 20
WHERE  employee_id = 103;

c065.front: What happens when you use CURRVAL before NEXTVAL?
c065.back: Error ORA-08002. CURRVAL shows the last NEXTVAL value of your session. If there has been no NEXTVAL in this session yet, there is nothing to show.

c066.front: After ROLLBACK, does a sequence number go back to the pool?
c066.back: No. A sequence does not roll back with the transaction. A number that was taken is lost, so gaps in the numbering are normal (for example after ROLLBACK or after cached values are lost).

c067.front: When does Oracle create an index by itself?
c067.back: For PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE, unless a matching index already exists, in which case it uses that one. For FOREIGN KEY Oracle creates no index; you must create it yourself.
c067.try_sql:
-- PK and UNIQUE have an index (INDEX_NAME), foreign keys (R) have none
SELECT constraint_name, constraint_type, index_name
FROM   user_constraints
WHERE  table_name = 'EMPLOYEES'
AND    constraint_type IN ('P', 'U', 'R')
ORDER  BY constraint_type, constraint_name;

c068.back: An index that is still maintained on every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, but the optimizer ignores it by default. You switch it with ALTER INDEX and VISIBLE / INVISIBLE.

c069.front: Who sees the data in a global temporary table?
c069.back: Only your session: each session sees only its own rows. ON COMMIT DELETE ROWS: the rows disappear at COMMIT (they live until the end of the transaction). ON COMMIT PRESERVE ROWS: they stay until the end of the session.

c070.back: A read-only table whose data lies in files on the server, not in the database. Oracle reads them through a DIRECTORY object and an access driver (ORACLE_LOADER or ORACLE_DATAPUMP).

c600.front: Private vs public synonym: how do they differ?
c600.back: A private synonym lives in your schema and needs the CREATE SYNONYM privilege. A public one belongs to PUBLIC, everyone sees it, and it needs CREATE PUBLIC SYNONYM. No synonym gives privileges on the object it points to.

c601.front: Where does Oracle look for a name given without a schema (for example SELECT * FROM emp)?
c601.back: First in your schema (tables, views, sequences, private synonyms), and only then among the public synonyms. Two objects with the same name in your schema are not allowed: ORA-00955.
c601.try_sql:
-- DUAL is not in your schema: the name resolves to the public synonym, and that to SYS.DUAL
SELECT owner, object_name, object_type
FROM   all_objects
WHERE  object_name = 'DUAL'
ORDER  BY owner;

c602.front: What if a synonym points to an object that does not exist?
c602.back: CREATE SYNONYM succeeds: Oracle does not check the target. The error appears only when it is used: ORA-00980: synonym translation is no longer valid.

c603.front: What are the defaults of CREATE SEQUENCE? What can ALTER SEQUENCE not change?
c603.back: Defaults: START WITH 1, INCREMENT BY 1, NOCYCLE, CACHE 20. ALTER cannot change START WITH (ORA-02283) and cannot set MAXVALUE below the current value (ORA-04009). With CYCLE the sequence starts again from MINVALUE, not from START WITH.

c604.front: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW, ALTER VIEW and FORCE: what does each do?
c604.back: OR REPLACE changes the view's query and keeps the granted privileges. ALTER VIEW only recompiles the view (COMPILE) or manages its constraints; it does not change the query. FORCE creates the view even when the base tables are missing; the view is then INVALID.

c605.back: An index on the result of an expression, for example CREATE INDEX i ON t (UPPER(col)). It helps conditions with the same expression, for example WHERE UPPER(col) = 'KING'. In USER_INDEXES it has INDEX_TYPE 'FUNCTION-BASED NORMAL', and the expression is in USER_IND_EXPRESSIONS.

c1600.back: The PUBLIC group (ALL_SYNONYMS.OWNER = 'PUBLIC'), not the user who created it. USER_SYNONYMS shows only your private synonyms.

c1601.front: How do you make an existing synonym point to another object?
c1601.back: CREATE OR REPLACE [PUBLIC] SYNONYM s FOR new_target. ALTER SYNONYM cannot change the target (ORA-00922), and a plain CREATE raises ORA-00955, because the name is already taken.

c1602.front: DROP SYNONYM name, when only a public synonym with that name exists: what happens?
c1602.back: Error ORA-01434: private synonym to be dropped does not exist. Without the word PUBLIC, Oracle looks only for a private synonym. You drop a public one with DROP PUBLIC SYNONYM (you also need that privilege).

c1603.front: What happens to a synonym when its table is dropped and then created again?
c1603.back: While the table is missing, the synonym has STATUS INVALID and using it raises ORA-00980. When an object with that name exists again, the synonym simply works and becomes VALID. There is no need to create it again.

c1604.front: Can you run INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE through a synonym?
c1604.back: Yes. Oracle replaces the synonym with the real object, so INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE change the base table. Privileges on that table are still needed.

c1605.front: IDENTITY column: ALWAYS vs BY DEFAULT vs BY DEFAULT ON NULL: what is the difference?
c1605.back: ALWAYS: you may not supply your own value (ORA-32795) or change it with UPDATE (ORA-32796). BY DEFAULT: a sequence number only when you leave the column out; an explicit NULL raises ORA-01400. BY DEFAULT ON NULL: NULL is replaced with the next number.

c1606.front: What does Oracle create for an IDENTITY column?
c1606.back: A system sequence named ISEQ$$_nnnnn (visible in USER_SEQUENCES and USER_TAB_IDENTITY_COLS). It disappears with the table. The column is NOT NULL at once. A table can have only one IDENTITY column (ORA-30669).

c1607.front: A column has DEFAULT seq.NEXTVAL, and someone dropped the sequence. What then?
c1607.back: Every INSERT that leaves out this column fails with ORA-02289: sequence does not exist. DATA_DEFAULT in USER_TAB_COLUMNS still shows the sequence's name.

c1608.front: You add a UNIQUE/PK constraint, and an index on those columns already exists. What does Oracle do?
c1608.back: It uses the existing index (even a non-unique one) and creates no new one. USER_CONSTRAINTS.INDEX_NAME shows that index. From then on, DROP INDEX on it raises ORA-02429.
c1608.try_sql:
-- INDEX_NAME in USER_CONSTRAINTS shows the index the PK/UNIQUE constraint uses
SELECT c.constraint_name, c.constraint_type, c.index_name, i.uniqueness
FROM   user_constraints c
JOIN   user_indexes i ON i.index_name = c.index_name
WHERE  c.constraint_type IN ('P', 'U')
ORDER  BY c.constraint_name;

c1609.front: Can you have two indexes on the same columns?
c1609.back: Only when they differ in something (for example one is UNIQUE and the other is not) and at most one of them is visible (VISIBLE). Otherwise you get ORA-01408: such column list already indexed.

c1610.front: How do you drop a primary key but keep its index?
c1610.back: ALTER TABLE t DROP PRIMARY KEY KEEP INDEX. Without KEEP INDEX, Oracle also drops the index it created for the key.

c1611.front: How do you do a Top-N (for example the 3 lowest salaries) with ROWNUM?
c1611.back: Sort first in a subquery (inline view), then filter outside: SELECT * FROM (SELECT ... ORDER BY sal) WHERE ROWNUM <= 3. When ROWNUM and ORDER BY are in the same query, ROWNUM is assigned before the sort and you get 3 arbitrary rows.
